questions.stem: A student writes about a novel narrated in the first person by a bitter teenager: 'The author hates her mother.' The main error is that she:
options: confuses the first-person narrator with the protagonist of the novel
mixes up the novel's context of production with its context of reception
treats the narrator, a constructed voice, as if it were the author
uses the present tense, when literary analysis is written in the past tense
questions.explanation: A first-person narrator is a constructed voice whose views may differ from, or be judged by, the author. The present tense, not the past, is the convention for literary analysis; here the narrator is the protagonist, and the sentence says nothing about context.

questions.stem: In formal literary analysis, after naming an author in full once, you usually refer to her by:
options: 'Ms' and her surname
her first name alone
her surname alone
her full name each time
questions.explanation: Literary criticism refers to writers by surname after the first full mention. Repeating the full name is clumsy, first names are overfamiliar, and titles such as 'Ms' are not the convention.

questions.stem: Which follows the usual convention for titles in a typed essay?
options: both titles in italics, since each one is the title of a complete text
a poem's title in quotation marks and a novel's title in italics
a novel's title in quotation marks and a poem's title in italics
both titles in quotation marks, since each one names a published work
questions.explanation: Longer, complete works such as novels and plays are italicised (underlined when handwritten), while shorter works such as poems and short stories go in quotation marks. Treating both kinds of title the same way ignores this distinction.

questions.stem: A student leaves out some words from the middle of a quotation. The convention is to mark the omission with:
options: a forward slash
a dash
an ellipsis
square brackets
questions.explanation: Three dots (an ellipsis) show that words have been left out of a quotation. Square brackets mark words the writer has added or changed, a slash marks a line break in quoted poetry, and a dash does not signal an omission.

questions.stem: Which sentence analyses a technique rather than merely identifying it?
options: Sibilance, alliteration and imagery all appear in 'silent, sliding snow' in line three.
The sibilance of 'silent, sliding snow' muffles the scene, echoing the speaker's numbness.
The poet uses sibilance in 'silent, sliding snow', repeating the s sound three times in the line.
The sibilance of 'silent, sliding snow' is a powerful technique that engages the reader.
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what a feature does and how it connects to meaning. Locating and describing a technique, listing several, or calling one 'powerful' without saying how it works shows recognition but not interpretation.

questions.stem: 'Through the rain, past the locked gates, beyond the last lamp, she ran.' The main clause is delayed until the end. This is:
options: a loose sentence
a sentence fragment
a balanced sentence
a periodic sentence
questions.explanation: A periodic sentence holds back its main clause until the end, building suspense. A loose sentence puts the main clause first, a fragment lacks a main clause and a balanced sentence sets two parallel halves against each other.

questions.stem: 'She packed, locked the door, walked away.' Leaving out the conjunctions between the actions is called:
options: anaphora
asyndeton
polysyndeton
tricolon
questions.explanation: Asyndeton omits conjunctions, often for speed or abruptness. Polysyndeton adds extra conjunctions, a tricolon is a group of three parallel parts (present here, but not the name for the omission) and anaphora repeats a word at the start of successive clauses.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses stylistic terminology most accurately?
options: The narrator's clipped sentences use pathetic fallacy to convey her restraint.
The narrator's clipped, paratactic sentences convey her emotional restraint.
The narrator's clipped, hypotactic sentences convey her emotional restraint.
The narrator's clipped, enjambed sentences convey her emotional restraint.
questions.explanation: Parataxis places clauses side by side without subordination, which fits clipped, restrained prose. Hypotaxis is heavy subordination, the opposite of clipped; enjambment describes verse lines; and pathetic fallacy attributes human feeling to nature or weather.

questions.stem: To support the claim that a novel's setting reflects its protagonist's isolation, which evidence is strongest?
options: the repeated image of the empty highway each time she drives home alone
the protagonist telling her sister, 'I have never felt so alone in my life'
a critic's review calling the novel 'a profound study of modern loneliness'
the author's remark that she grew up in a similar remote country town
questions.explanation: The strongest evidence is a specific textual detail that directly supports the claim, especially a recurring one. The protagonist's line shows isolation but not the setting, and a review or the author's biography does not show how the setting works in the text.

questions.stem: In a timed essay, a student has five good examples for one paragraph. The most effective approach is usually to:
options: hold the extra examples back for the conclusion to end on new evidence
analyse two or three of them in depth rather than list all five briefly
give each of the five one sentence of analysis so that none is wasted
focus on the one strongest example and set the other four aside
questions.explanation: Depth of analysis earns more than a catalogue of examples: two or three well-chosen pieces of evidence, closely analysed, build a convincing argument. A sentence each is still a list, a single example can leave the claim thinly supported, and a conclusion should not introduce new evidence.

questions.stem: A student argues that a novel endorses greed because its narrator praises a rich banker throughout. Which objection is strongest?
options: today's readers condemn greed, so the novel must be read as condemning it too
the narrator is just one character, so his opinions tell us nothing about the novel's values
the narrator's praise may be ironic, and the text can invite readers to judge the narrator
the author's own views are unknown, so the novel's values cannot be determined
questions.explanation: A narrator's view is not necessarily the text's: details can expose a narrator's blindness, so the implied author may be critiquing greed. Values are inferred from the text, not from biography or from today's readers, and a narrator's opinions are evidence to weigh rather than ignore.

questions.stem: An effective conclusion to a literary essay:
options: restates the thesis word for word so that the marker sees that it was proved
presents the essay's strongest quotation, saved for the final word
summarises each body paragraph in turn, in the order they appeared
draws the argument together and reflects on the text's wider significance
questions.explanation: A conclusion synthesises the argument and may consider why the text matters. Repeating the thesis word for word or summarising paragraph by paragraph adds little, and new evidence belongs in the body.

questions.stem: Which topic sentence best sets up an argument about how a poem's form shapes its meaning?
options: The poem's shrinking stanzas are an example of form, a key aspect of any poem.
The speaker's narrowing hope is conveyed through the poem's bleak winter imagery.
The poem's stanzas shrink from six lines to two as the poem moves towards its end.
The poem's stanzas shrink from six lines to two, enacting the speaker's narrowing hope.
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence makes an arguable claim linking a specific formal feature to meaning. Describing the stanza pattern or labelling it 'form' gives no interpretation, and a claim about imagery argues about language rather than form.

questions.stem: A student writes a review of a novel for the school magazine instead of an essay for her teacher. Which change is most appropriate?
options: use more critical terminology, since magazine readers expect expertise
avoid revealing the ending and finish with a clear recommendation for readers
summarise the whole plot first so that readers who have not read it can follow
keep the essay's formal thesis and topic sentences, adding a star rating
questions.explanation: Analytical texts take different forms for different audiences: a review evaluates for readers who may not have read the book, so it avoids spoilers and recommends. A full plot summary gives away the ending, and an essay's formal structure and dense terminology suit the teacher's task instead.

questions.stem: A reader writes: 'The narration invites sympathy for her while quietly exposing her self-deception.' Compared with 'I felt her loneliness as if it were my own', this response is more:
options: empathetic, identifying closely with the main character's feelings
resistant, rejecting the values that the narration invites readers to share
evaluative, judging how well the novel is written as a whole
critical, stepping back to examine how the text shapes responses
questions.explanation: Responses range from empathetic, which identifies with a character, to critical, which examines how the text constructs that identification. The first comment analyses the narration's effect without rejecting the text's values or rating its quality; the second shares feeling.

questions.stem: A student first finds a poem simply 'depressing'. After reading a critical essay on its seasonal imagery, she argues that it moves from despair towards renewal. This shows:
options: her personal response being replaced by the critic's more authoritative reading
a resistant reading that rejects the values the poem first seemed to promote
a change in the poem's meaning caused by a new context of reception
critical reading developing an initial response into a more complex interpretation
questions.explanation: Reading criticism can extend and deepen a first personal response without replacing it: her own reading has grown, not been swapped for the critic's. She does not reject the poem's values, and the poem itself has not changed.

questions.stem: A student writes a short story from the point of view of a lighthouse that has watched a town for a century. This choice most likely:
options: creates an unreliable narrator whose account readers are meant to distrust
turns the story into an allegory in which the lighthouse stands for God
offers a long, detached view that makes human worries seem brief
gives intimate access to each townsperson's private thoughts and motives
questions.explanation: An unusual narrator gives a distinctive perspective: a century-long, non-human vantage point puts human concerns in proportion. A watcher sees from outside rather than reading minds, and being non-human makes a narrator neither unreliable nor allegorical by default.

questions.stem: A student wants an imaginative piece to capture a single, intense moment of grief. Which form suits this purpose best?
options: an epistolary novella of letters written over a year
a short lyric poem or a brief prose vignette
a ballad narrating the events that led to the death
a short story tracing the illness through to the funeral
questions.explanation: Lyric poems and vignettes focus on one moment and its feeling. A ballad, a story spanning an illness or a year of letters follows events over time rather than holding a single moment.

questions.stem: A student's imaginative piece about a school's closure aims to be wry rather than mournful. Which line fits this tone?
options: The bell rang one last time, and all our childhoods died with its echo.
The bell rang one last time, a sound we would carry for the rest of our lives.
The bell rang one last time, shrill and furious, like an alarm warning of fire.
The bell rang one last time, as if it too had somewhere better to be.
questions.explanation: Wry tone mixes humour with feeling; personifying the bell as impatient undercuts sadness with irony. The other lines are melodramatic, nostalgic or angry, with no humour to temper them.

questions.stem: A student's story about a long friendship is told in five short scenes, each set at the same bus stop years apart. This structure mainly:
options: creates a non-linear timeline that readers must put back in order
suggests that the friends are trapped and unable to leave their town
makes the setting, rather than the friendship, the story's real subject
uses one fixed place so that the changes between the friends stand out
questions.explanation: A constant setting works like a control in an experiment: what changes is the friendship, which the repetition highlights. The scenes move forward in time, nothing implies the friends never leave, and the place serves the friendship rather than replacing it as the subject.

questions.stem: A student wants a line describing a storm to sound harsh and violent. Which line uses sound most effectively?
options: Cracked branches clattered, crashed and cut the dark.
Wild winds whirled and wailed with weary, woeful whines.
Sheets of silver rain swept swiftly over the sleeping shore.
The storm was loud and violent and frightening and fierce.
questions.explanation: Hard consonant sounds such as the repeated k sound create a harsh, percussive effect that suits violence. Alliteration alone is not enough: soft w and s sounds murmur, and a string of adjectives tells readers the storm is violent rather than letting them hear it.

questions.stem: A student is creating a short graphic story. To show a character's growing isolation, which visual choice is most effective?
options: a close-up of her face in each panel to show her loneliness in detail
thought bubbles in which she reflects that she has no friends left
dark colours and heavy rain in each panel to mirror her sadness
panels in which she grows smaller and the empty space around her grows
questions.explanation: Visual devices such as scale and negative space can convey isolation without words. Close-ups keep her central and fill the frame, thought bubbles tell rather than show, and rain and dark colours suggest sadness rather than isolation.

questions.stem: A student's imaginative text set in 1950s Brisbane must represent its time convincingly without lecturing readers. Which choice works best?
options: period details woven into action, such as the milkman's dawn round and a family at the wireless
a narrator who pauses to explain each detail of 1950s life for readers today
dialogue in the formal style of a Victorian novel, to sound old-fashioned
footnotes explaining the period's products, slang and events as they appear
questions.explanation: Representations of time and place are most convincing when details arise naturally in the action. An explaining narrator or footnotes lecture readers, and Victorian dialogue belongs to the wrong period.

questions.stem: A student revises 'The water rose slowly' to 'The water rose, and rose, and would not stop rising.' The revision mainly:
options: uses onomatopoeia to imitate the sound of the flood
uses hyperbole to exaggerate the flood for comic effect
uses repetition and rhythm to build a sense of dread
uses polysyndeton to slow the pace and calm the scene
questions.explanation: Repeating 'rose' and adding 'and' between clauses creates a relentless rhythm that mirrors the rising water. The polysyndeton builds momentum rather than calm, nothing imitates a sound, and the effect is menacing, not comic.

questions.stem: A student writes a bedtime story for young children that gently carries a message about grief. Which choice best suits both the audience and the purpose?
options: a realistic story of a grandparent's death in hospital, told in close detail
a gentle animal tale in which a little fox learns ways to remember a lost friend
a rhyming tale in which a lost puppy is found safe and well on the last page
a gentle fable that ends with the moral 'Do not be sad when friends go away'
questions.explanation: Form, content and tone must suit audience and purpose: an animal tale is familiar to young children and lets the message come gently. A story in which the puppy is found avoids loss, a moral telling children not to be sad dismisses grief, and detailed hospital realism is too confronting for the audience.

questions.stem: While drafting a short story, a student realises that her ending contradicts the narrator's established voice. The best next step is to:
options: revise the ending or the voice so that the story is consistent
proofread the ending carefully, since voice errors are surface mistakes
keep the ending and explain the shift in her written reflection
leave the shift, since a change of voice adds variety to a story
questions.explanation: Drafting and redrafting aim at a coherent text, so an inconsistent voice needs revision. Proofreading fixes surface errors, not structural problems, a reflection cannot repair the story itself, and an unmotivated shift reads as inconsistency rather than variety.

questions.stem: Proofreading a literary essay should include checking that:
options: the thesis is repeated at the start of each body paragraph
quotations are copied exactly as they appear in the text
quotations are reworded in your own words to show understanding
each paragraph uses the same TEEL pattern as the one before it
questions.explanation: Quotations must be accurate, since analysis depends on the exact words. Paraphrasing defeats the purpose of quoting, and paragraph formulas or a repeated thesis are matters of structure, not proofreading, and are not requirements.
